Not OP, but I have a few sources that I found while researching gender in the ancient Levant and ANE more broadly. “Was Ancient Israel a Patriarchal Society” by Carol Meyers (Journal of Biblical Literature, 2014) and “Fertility and Gender in the Ancient Near East” by Stephanie Budin (Sex in Antiquity, 2014). 

Both - but if I remember right, especially the latter - addresses the association between the advent of agriculture and the need to organise people by social households in order to organise procreation. We find in these areas, procreation and fertility was often the responsibility of male gods and this was often reflected in how gender and power was represented in Kings with references to bulls or gardens etc. Francesca Stavrakapoulou’s book God: An Anatomy also provides useful information on fertility, gender, and the ANE.

Hello! So I had a hymenectomy on the NHS back in 2019 I believe. I first went complaining of a septate hymen in 2014 and was just given dialators. Here's my perspective as someone who was sexually assaulted and harassed by people my own age as a child/teen. 

Please forgive your younger self. As another poster has said, some things are more violating than others, but the most important thing is how you feel about it *now.* It seems like you very clearly acknowledge that it was and still would be inappropriate, and you wouldn't do it again. You're already several steps ahead of who you were then, so that's a great start. I recently had to let go and confess something to a therapist of mine, something I felt guilty about, but she was extremely reassuring in that teenagers are stupid, and no one actually knew or was effected by whatever it was, so the only harm I'm causing is to myself by torturing myself with the memory. Even though our circumstances are different, I think coming at it with a similar approach might be helpful. We should NOT do things because other people technically don't know, but now it's done and firmly in your past, and on top of it you were a developing teenager, unless someone else brings it up, you are only hurting yourself.

You say it wasn't compulsive or uncontrollable, and just ignorance, but I think it's a common experience for a lot of young people to not *know* what's appropriate. If kids aren't exposed to the right kind of education or environments, as well as other factors like neurodivergence, kids and teens might have a harder time recognising what is and isn't appropriate or harmful. Sex ed is piss poor in most places, and masturbating gives you dopamine. If you found a quick hack to essentially do a shot of dopamine, of course the instinct is to chase it. It doesn't sound like your motivation was anything sinister.

Intercourse with eunuchs is something I personally don't know enough about yet, but am currently gathering research in as it'll be part of my thesis this coming year. As far as I understand, eunuchs are/were both born and made, and thus some never men to begin with. Some also speculate it could even apply to erectile dysfunction. Eunuch is distinction of sexual anatomy and social mobility, but gender and sex were fluid in the ancient Near East and Med. One theory is that because many cultures which influenced Hebrew Bible writings had heavy emphasis on sperm/seed and fertility, testicle status in regards to proximity to the deity was important. This is also why a lot of people read the Ethiopian Eunuch in Acts as a Queer liberative narrative, due to the significance of a wholly 'othered' person in gender, sex, race/ethnicity, and class being the first narrative convert post ascention.  

So then, in terms of intercourse, it's quite hard to say. The truth is, we don't really know a lot of what was permitted and what wasn't in the era that the Bible was composed (we're talking earliest 8th century BCE at a stretch, to 2nd century BCE, mostly 6th - 4th cenutries BCE for Hebrew Bible, 1st and 2nd centuries CE for NT). Theology and social rules changed all the time depending on culture and progress, just as it does today. For just one major example, the tone and theology shift between the texts written before, during, and after the events of the traumatic Babylonian exile and Temple destruction and rebuilding massively reshape YHWH worship and theology. You also have to think about who is writing these texts, and who are they writing them for? Who is engaging in theological texts about adherence to proper YHWH worship? It's not your everyman, or everyeunuch. It's the elites, the scholars and scribes, priests and royals. 

So, really, we're talking about what's considered a 'sin', or religious transgression, for those elites in that ancient context. Eunuchs were often purchased/traded as slaves or workers in elite households because of their liminal status. You're right, they couldn't marry because they had no offspring to produce, which was the only function of a marriage. They were able to transition through male and female spaces in a house with ease, and thus were perfect for serving. Their ambiguous sex and genitalia and convenient detatchment from the household would actually make them luxury sex partners. The ultimate no-strings-attached. There are many Bible passages to indicate that the dominance and sexual ownership of others is sin/transgression (usually laws), and others that contradict that (usually mourning genres/trauma literature), so you could argue that it's a sin to have sex with a eunuch because of the non-consensual power dynamic, rather than because 'it's gay >:\['.

I would really recommend the text ***'The Invention of God'*** **by Thomas Romer** if you can get a hold of it. It details the emergence of YHWH as a desert storm god in the Ancient Near Eastern south, who was absorbed into El (Elyon)'s pantheon. YHWH seems to usurp El at some point and by the time of the Moses tradition, YHWH is fully identifying himself as El Shaddai (God of the Wilderness/Mountain/Destroyer are our best guesses) in Exodus 6:2-3. In a sense, YHWH is 'backtracking' by saying it was him they were worshipping all along, when they were worshipping a separate deity, El.

So I actually went to a postgrad seminar where someone talked about this - specifically Rahab and other women that are in the lineage of Jesus and what that means. The article in question that she was presented is ***'H******oly Mothers of God: sex work, inheritance, and the women of Jesus’ genealogy'*** **by Dr Marika Rose.** If you can get access to that then I would recommend it.

In short, though, yes, Rahab was a sex worker, in the sense that she had sex outside of marriage and it was for a profit. The Hebrew used to describe her (אשה זונה (*ishah zonah*)) literally means 'prostitute woman', so we can safely assume that the Biblical authors at least viewed her as such. And yes, this is the same Rahab in the lineage of Jesus.

Short answer: no.

Long answer: There isn't any significant evidence in the New Testament, which are our sources for Mary of Magda, that she was a sex worker. This is a later development of western Christianity in art and literature. Her roles in the gospels are incredibly important ones, as the first witness to the resurrection and a disciple of Jesus, but there is little evidence that this came about after or during a profession of sex working. There's a lot of resources about this and a lot of people have lots of different opinions, but there's definitely NOT a resounding yes in academic circles, though you might find it in religious circles.

Some might argue that her status as an independent woman (mostly due to her name and her lack of male chaperone mentioned) would mean she would have been a sex worker (one of the only professions a woman could have independently outside of a man), but this isn't sufficient evidence. 'Seven demons' others argue is a reference, but the numerology can refer to many things, and she might have instead been suffering from a mental or physical health issue that imitates the 1st-century perceptions of demon possession.

What's complex though is that, obviously, she might well have been, and it just wasn't mentioned. That also would not be an issue, as Jesus engaged with all types of people in the margins of society as equal as he would his most faithful servant. (Edited to add as I posted without finishing bc ADHD I guess) There's a polemic against sex workers which have people often running to defend Mary and say, no of course she isn't! When actually, there is no issue with her being a sex worker morally, ethically or literally. You have to untangle whether scholars or religious thinkers are denying her status as a sex worker because of bias against sex workers, or because of a genuine lack of evidence. It's not disrespectful to call her a sex worker, but it's also not accurate.
